clue.text: The way to heaven for Israel-to be

definitions.text: The way to heaven for Israel-to be

parts.words: The way to heaven for Israel-to be
parts.note: the patriarch Jacob, later renamed Israel, dreamt of a ladder reaching up to heaven in Genesis

explanation.surface: A question of how a future nation might find its route to paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'Israel-to-be': Jacob was renamed Israel after wrestling with the angel, so the man who would become Israel is Jacob, and his dream showed a ladder up to heaven.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the patriarch dreams of a stairway with angels going up to heaven, which tradition names after him.

clue.text: No prison-builder in Mississippi City?

parts.note: a man of stone walls who builds no prison, recalling the Confederate general nicknamed Stonewall, gives the surname of the state capital of Mississippi

explanation.surface: A query about whether a Southern city ever built its own jail.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Lovelace wrote 'Stone walls do not a prison make', so a stone-wall man is no prison-builder: that is the Civil War general Stonewall, whose surname is shared by the capital of Mississippi.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital city of the US state of Mississippi carries this name, as did the general called Stonewall.

clue.text: Sabotaging oil race causes some heat

indicators.note: sabotage wrecks something, so the letters of these words are wrecked and rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Wrecking a motor race with spilt oil generates a bit of heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sabotaging' rearranges OIL RACE.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit used to measure heat energy, so one of them is a small quantity of warmth.

clue.text: Glass that may fall without risk of breaking

definitions.text: Glass that may fall without risk of breaking

parts.words: Glass that may fall without risk of breaking
parts.note: glass here is the old household name for a weather instrument whose reading falls when pressure drops, with no shattering involved

explanation.surface: A tumbler that can be dropped safely without shattering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glass' suggests a drinking vessel, but an old name for the household pressure gauge is the glass, and the glass 'falls' when bad weather is coming.
explanation.definitionFit: A weather instrument, traditionally called the glass, whose reading falls as atmospheric pressure drops.

clue.text: The king is dead? Not yet

parts.note: the late king is the dead one
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: The traditional proclamation of a monarch's death is cut short with a demurral.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes 'The king is dead, long live the king'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done afterwards, at some subsequent time, has not happened yet.

clue.text: Denry Machin holds its rise to be violent

indicators.note: in a down clue, a rise reads the whole result from the bottom upwards
one word holding another takes it inside, so the novel's title wraps round the word its

parts.note: Denry Machin is the hero of Arnold Bennett's novel The Card, a card being a lively wag

explanation.surface: A character in an Edwardian novel manages to contain his ambitions so as to be fierce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' puts ITS inside CARD to make CITSARD, and 'rise' reads that upwards in this down entry. Denry Machin is the hero of Arnold Bennett's novel The Card.
explanation.definitionFit: Extreme and forceful measures are harsh or severe, like violent ones.

clue.text: Cost of stocking the river with birds

indicators.note: a river stocking fish holds them within it, so the river name holds the birds

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, a crossword favourite
pens are female swans

explanation.surface: How much it costs to stock a river with waterfowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stocking' puts PENS inside EXE; the Exe is a river in south-west England and pens are female swans.
explanation.definitionFit: Money spent on something is its outlay or price.

clue.text: One who should get phrase right on transcription?

definitions.text: One who should get phrase right on transcription?

indicators.note: a transcription renders material in another form, so these letters are written out again in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A secretary taking shorthand ought to record each phrase accurately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transcription' rearranges GET PHRASE plus R (right) plus ON; the whole clue also describes the shorthand writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A shorthand writer's job is to take down speech word for word, so accuracy is expected of them.

clue.text: Mrs Gargery's cane did not make Pip laugh

definitions.text: Mrs Gargery's cane did not make Pip laugh

parts.words: Mrs Gargery's cane did not make Pip laugh
parts.note: in Dickens's Great Expectations, Pip's sister beats him with a cane she ironically calls by a name suggesting something that causes giggles

explanation.surface: A grim scene from Great Expectations: the boy's punishment was no laughing matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Joe Gargery, Pip's sister in Great Expectations, names her cane after something that ought to make you laugh, but it only hurts.
explanation.definitionFit: That is the name Dickens gives the cane; a feather that provokes laughter carries the same word.

clue.text: Put one's foot down on 4, irregularly holding member

indicators.note: the scrambled letters hold the member, wrapping round it
irregular arrangement means the letters of that answer are scrambled

parts.note: 4 refers to the answer to 4 down
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Laying down the law on a matter of timing while keeping hold of a limb.
explanation.walkthrough: 4 is the answer to 4 down; 'irregularly' rearranges it as TRALE, and 'holding' puts MP inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To stamp down heavily on something, crushing it underfoot.

clue.text: An endless circle of stones

parts.note: a band set with gems all the way round, unbroken, given as a symbol of everlasting love

explanation.surface: A prehistoric stone ring with no beginning or end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circle of stones' suggests Stonehenge, but the stones are gems set right round a finger band, symbolising love without end.
explanation.definitionFit: A band set with a continuous line of gems, given to symbolise everlasting love.

clue.text: Remedy found in no way strange

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way
rum is British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: A cure turns up in an unexpected fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: RUM is British slang for strange.
explanation.definitionFit: A quack medicine or pet scheme, offered as a cure-all.

clue.text: Sappers about to join in retreat in train

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the army's sappers

indicators.note: a retreat goes backwards, so the word for joining is read in reverse

parts.note: to unite is to join together

explanation.surface: Army engineers are about to link up during a withdrawal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' reads UNITE backwards as ETINU; RE is the Royal Engineers. 'about' simply links.
explanation.definitionFit: A train is the band of attendants following an important person, an entourage.

clue.text: Unusually green sort of painting

indicators.note: in an unusual way means the letters are arranged out of their usual order

explanation.surface: A rather oddly coloured style of art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusually' rearranges GREEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Genre painting depicts scenes of everyday life, one category of art.

clue.text: Run about in the cricket side for the club

indicators.note: these letters go in, splitting the word the

parts.note: taken as written
C is short for circa, about
the on side is the leg side of a cricket field

explanation.surface: A fielder dashes around within his team's half of the pitch to reach the bat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts RUN plus C (circa, about) inside THE; ON is the leg side in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A short heavy stick carried by police as a weapon is a cudgel.

clue.text: Disinterested like the little people following us abroad

indicators.note: the fairy word comes after the foreign one

parts.note: uns is German for us
elfish means like elves, the fairy folk

explanation.surface: Being impartial, like fairies trailing behind travelling tourists.
explanation.walkthrough: UNS is German for 'us'; 'following' puts ELFISH after it.
explanation.definitionFit: In its strict sense disinterested means having no personal stake, putting others first.

clue.text: Composer runs into French friends, afloat in tropical seas

indicators.note: these letters go into the French word for friends

parts.note: amis is French for friends
Alban Berg was an Austrian composer
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A musician bumps into some Parisian pals while sailing in warm waters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' puts BERG plus R inside AMIS.
explanation.definitionFit: The waxy substance from sperm whales is found floating in warm oceans, prized in perfumery.

clue.text: Harris for instance as one of three

definitions.text: Harris for instance as one of three

parts.words: Harris for instance as one of three
parts.note: Harris is one of the trio in Jerome K. Jerome's comic novel about three men rowing up the Thames

explanation.surface: Someone named Harris counted as one of a trio.
explanation.walkthrough: Harris is one of Jerome K. Jerome's Three Men in a Boat, so he is a man of the boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A rower or oarsman, as Harris was on the Thames trip in the comic novel.

clue.text: An excellent specimen of a snake

definitions.meaning: an old informal word for a first-rate example of something
a short name for the venomous American viper with a noisy tail

explanation.surface: A fine example of a serpent.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally a cracker or corker, and also short for the rattlesnake.

clue.text: In saying the right thing one is implied

indicators.note: the numeral goes in the word for diplomacy

parts.note: tact is the knack of saying the right thing
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Saying the right thing is understood without being spelt out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts I inside TACT.
explanation.definitionFit: Understood without being stated, unspoken.

clue.text: Two items on the afternoon menu — or one?

parts.words: Two items on the afternoon menu
parts.note: a hot drink served at four o'clock

parts.words: Two items on the afternoon menu
parts.note: a sweet baked item served at the same meal

explanation.surface: Two things offered at afternoon tea, or just one of them?
explanation.walkthrough: The two items are a drink and a cake; joined they name a single toasted bun eaten at the same meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A light yeast bun, often toasted and buttered, served as part of afternoon tea.

clue.text: A time-server such as Magwitch?

definitions.meaning: a prisoner serving a sentence, doing time
Magwitch is the escaped prisoner of Dickens's Great Expectations

explanation.surface: A self-seeker resembling the Dickens character Magwitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A prisoner serving a sentence, as Abel Magwitch was, transported to Australia.

clue.text: Cheer up! Listen to X

parts.note: to hear is to listen to
X is the Roman numeral ten

explanation.surface: An exhortation to be happy and to attend to someone called X.
explanation.walkthrough: X is the Roman numeral for ten.
explanation.definitionFit: To encourage or raise someone's spirits.

clue.text: Standard article for the opera

parts.note: a norm is a standard
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Usual merchandise for an opera house.
explanation.walkthrough: The opera is Bellini's, named after its Druid priestess heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Bellini's 1831 opera about a Druid priestess bears this title.

clue.text: Pound wage for this apprentice?

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for the pound sterling, from libra
an earner is informal British slang for a source of income

explanation.surface: Is a pound a week the going rate for a trainee?
explanation.walkthrough: L stands for pound (libra); 'a nice little earner' is British slang for something that brings in money.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainee or novice still being taught a trade.

clue.text: Rose — an incoherent speaker

definitions.meaning: a climbing variety of the garden flower

explanation.surface: Someone named Rose is a poor public speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A climbing rose variety, and also someone who wanders off the point when talking.

clue.text: The last alternative nationality Englishman Ralph Rackstraw refused

definitions.text: The last alternative nationality Englishman Ralph Rackstraw refused

parts.words: The last alternative nationality Englishman Ralph Rackstraw refused
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore the sailor might have been Russian, French, Turk or Prussian, or perhaps a man from Rome, yet remains an Englishman

explanation.surface: A sailor turned down several foreign citizenships, the final one included.
explanation.walkthrough: In HMS Pinafore the chorus sings that Ralph Rackstraw might have been a Roosian, a French, or Turk, or Proosian, 'or perhaps Itali-an', but remains an Englishman: the last option listed.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's final alternative nationality is that of someone from Rome or Milan.

clue.text: Trespass by men after, fish — caught ten perhaps at the outside

indicators.note: the jumbled ten sits outside, its letters split around the rest
perhaps signals that the letters of the word ten may be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the men come after the fish

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
a roach is a freshwater fish
taken as written

explanation.surface: Anglers intrude on private water, landing a catch of perhaps ten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges TEN as ENT, and 'at the outside' splits it as EN...T around C (caught) plus ROACH, with MEN placed 'after' the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: An intrusion onto someone else's land or rights.
